items.title: Open-source AI without Jensen
items.content: The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a major setback for the US development of an open model ecosystem. Nvidia still has the financial interests in supporting open models, which are to avoid concentration in power among a few customers who would develop their own chips and reduce Nvidia’s profits, but supporting the open ecosystem is a tricky puzzle more than an engineering problem to grind out a solution on. Nvidia’s business operations are famously extremely dependent on Jensen as an operator, so it is a consensus opinion that there are challenges ahead (or even more high-profile departures through chip-smuggling investigations or plain-old sharks circling more poachable talent). Nvidia’s number one goal is to stabilize the ship, deliver to customers in the next 24 months, and prevent implosion. Open models have been one of Jensen’s more ambitious, founder-style bets. He has been flooding the zone with funding in a way that will very likely dry up. Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. In this period, the open model economy is in its nascency. These are crucial years for establishing use-cases, revenue flow, and motives to continue training the next generation models. I discussed the sensitivity of these early years in my recent talk at Fireworks Forge ( slides , recording ). The core of the argument is one upside for open models, a reason to be optimistic, and one downside. The positive case is that the open model economy has correctly latched onto “ownership of intelligence” and enterprise post-training as a crucial lane. What is to be determined is exactly how big the downstream market is. The downside is that the true long-term benefit of open models, as truly commoditized intelligence, is very far from realization with compute in such short supply. In the near term, where inference startups are also struggling to get enough chips (because Anthropic and OpenAI are buying so much capacity), there’s little margin competition on open-weight models. If open-source models are also served at giant inference margins, as we learned with DeepSeek’s DeepInfer release, they’re far from a commodity. In this paradigm, the closed labs with better economies of scale and integration from model to datacenter and chips will win. I expanded on this challenge in my recent piece on the open model economy . Together, a lot still needs to go right for open models to be a meaningful economic engine. Jensen’s support, and protection, gave the ecosystem time to figure this out. Jensen was more than a cheerleader. He would stop a lot of shit from going wrong once early winds were stirring. He was willing to use his power on open models. There’s a major swell in Democratic government funding towards candidates that want to regulate the AI industry, fostering “safety” . Many of these people feel a need to do something and have general opinions that open models are unsafe, while not being educated on the complexities of their benefits. My biggest near-term worry is sloppy regulation at the state level, followed by national regulation. We’ve been one, strong Chinese open-weight model away from a crisis since this summer. It still holds – especially as we enter a new, turbulent equilibrium of cybersecurity. We have not seen a major hack driven by a popular Chinese open-weight model, but it is a matter of when, not if. We need someone to encourage caution and an ecosystem perspective when the “open-weight hawks” come hunting. Knocking over the open-source AI domino today is easy — if done, unwinding the downstream concentration of power, reduction in safety research, and stifling of long-term innovation is far harder. On public data, it looks like balancing long-term innovation versus short term risks, but this is due to how horribly hard it is to measure the open model economy (e.g. the most valuable aspects of it run on private infrastructure). It’s a recurring challenge facing the ecosystem and my work. As a brief aside, the extent to which the media ecosystem is revolving around timing today, rather than exact availability of information, is incredible. All of these Jensen affairs were known, but getting them out at the right time, right after the midterm political swing, took down the king. The same goes for the Jacob Coxon brouhaha this summer. All of that safety culture around top labs was well known, but the right timing around datacenters and the Overton window made it a national issue. This could very well happen at some point for open model safety, as it tends to be harm, risk, or safety-related narratives that drive the modern media algorithms. I cannot imagine my work on open-science driving such a media cycle, because it will never happen. Share The only lasting solution to this is to incubate a truly frontier open model player in the US. For example, I agree completely with Dylan Patel, CEO of SemiAnalysis, on a core problem in the US open model ecosystem. From a recent ChinaTalk + SemiAnalysis emergency podcast : Jordan Schneider: I do want your guys’ take on just how bad this is, that Jensen’s now off the table for the future of American innovation. And we should talk about open models. I mean, he was the big champion, right? Dylan, you were talking earlier — I still don’t understand quite why someone didn’t just spend a few billion dollars and make something better than Kimi or DeepSeek and open source it. Dylan Patel: Not that easy. It’s not money, it’s talent, man. All of the most talented people primarily work at Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind, and Meta TBD, right? And then those who don’t are split across a hundred different startups. I mean, yes, Thinking Machines has a cracked team, but is Thinking Machines as good as Moonshot

items.title: How big is the open model economy today?
items.content: My longest running agent testbed has been building the Interconnects Dashboard — an aggregator of all of the best data on open model adoption and performance from across the web. This dashboard is freely available and becoming quite useful. Still, all the measurements we have on open model adoption are incredibly imprecise. We have noisy platform metrics, marketing-related metrics from startups, and imperfect public evaluations. It takes an informed eye to figure out where things are going. These research notes are my current best approximations of where we stand. As with most things on Interconnects, our goal is to build well more value than we capture, so the data on the dashboard will remain free for the foreseeable future. These notes will be more raw than many of my articles, a place for sharing what I’m mulling over but don’t have complete evidence for (yet). They will be primarily paid, enabling me to speak more freely. If you work in AI policy or policy-facing research, please reach out to us and we can likely get discounted or free access. The primary question I wanted to address today is: What is the market for open model inference? Is it growing? Is it a rounding error relative to OpenAI/Anthropic? Share I’ve been building the best measurements I can here, primarily using the open model inference startups Baseten, Fireworks, and Together AI as the bellwethers here (along with the open model share of OpenRouter’s token volume, which they thankfully report in their API). The hyperscalers also likely have a major footprint here, e.g. Amazon Bedrock and Azure’s model garden, but I haven’t seen them break down usage by model category. The startups’ fates are much more directly correlated with the success of open model inference as a category. For the latest data, we can start with a slide from my talk on the open model economy (recording here ). These are the public disclosures from the open model startups on their token volume, over time, log-scale. This shows near-exponential growth, before the uptick that would follow GLM 5.2’s step change in open agents . For example, Fireworks announced at their first company conference this week that they’re serving more than 40T tokens per day to customers’ customized models. This is just one slice of their inference, a vertical that they said grew over 2x from this summer, so I would expect their total number this fall to be well above 100T tokens when we get the next update. My first instinct with these numbers has been to ground them versus any closed model or hyperscale company we can, at least in terms of token volume. Thankfully, Google releases token volumes for the entire platform and API usage in their earnings reports. items.title: Was I wrong about open models & cyber risks?
items.content: Last week coined the term “ Black October “ after an onslaught of critical vulnerability disclosures, including PHP2Shell and a long-standing GitLab bug, signified the moment when the cyber risks of AI models started to materialize. It seemed like the news cycle had stabilized a bit when I started writing this, but then there was news about another major crypto security incident at Binance . The crypto industry has a very long history of hacks , so it’s not the best industry to indicate vulnerabilities translating into new societal harm. Still, we are very much still living through the implications of this transition. The best guess for what is happening in the cybersecurity space is that the behind the scenes work has only accelerated, bringing more people and resources in to try and patch the internet — the Wall Street Journal reported that cyber first responders are strained , which seems like the system working. We’re living through this plot of an exponential rise in vulnerabilities, which will take a long time to level off at the top of the sigmoid. A few weeks ago, before the rapid acceleration in vulnerability disclosures and the uptick in reported hacks, I wrote the following take. It’s been getting a pretty consistent barrage of feedback, some hopeless dunk attempts and some reasonable discussion, so I wanted to unpack where I stand. Share Open-weight Mythos in April would’ve been fine? When Claude Mythos was announced, it was previewed as if it was a new class of cyber weapon, where if it ended up in the wrong hands it would’ve caused mass societal destabilization. It seems like this was wrong. By all measures, GLM-5.3 is the model that crosses that threshold of capability, and there’s little public evidence that much has changed, and we’re over a month out of the model weight release. In fact, I would go further. If Claude Mythos was accidentally released as open-weight, it seems like the world would have been more or less fine. Yes, there would be a clear increase in cybersecurity incidents and it would be bad for society if the model leaked, but it would be a scenario that looks more like an acceleration than a step change in risk. The leading proponents of this new wave of open-weight fear mongering have effectively been making a falsifiable prediction — that the current open-weight models are going to cause substantial, not seen before AI harms by crippling our cyber infrastructure. Based on all the evidence I have, which I’ve unpacked above, they’re set up to be wrong. At least now, after so many years of debating open weight risks, we will start to get some real answers. To start the reflection, I wanted to do more due diligence and track down some receipts on the claim that the AI safety community was reacting as if open-weight Mythos would be an actual disaster, and not just a painful headache. This was distinctly my impression having lived through the online discourse. I’ve gotten criticism that the frontier AI community never said it would be a “true disaster,” but regardless of exactly what they said, it is always about how people hear and internalize your information. Here are some examples of the sort of language that I felt was too exaggerated and from prominent people, which spilled into the public and more importantly federal government perspective that this was a cyber weapon include: Rob Wiblin, host of the 80,000 hours podcast, on his own podcast (April 10, 2026): “If it fell into the hands of criminals or hostile state cyber actors, it would be an actual disaster.” Anthropic, in the Project Glasswing announcement blog (April 7, 2026): “Given the rate of AI progress, it will not be long before such capabilities proliferate, potentially beyond actors who are committed to deploying them safely. The fallout—for economies, public safety, and national security—could be severe.” For one that is actually more reasonable, to illustrate the fine lines between correct and exaggerated, from Zvi Mowshowitz (who I don’t agree with a ton of things on) on April 9, 2026: “Claude Mythos would give attackers a cornucopia of zero-day exploits for essentially all the software on Earth … It would be chaos.” To date, this chaos has been confined to those running large-scale digital products, which is good, but could change. I largely still stand by my above writing a few weeks ago, but I’m nervous about it. I’m not a cyber expert, I’m working hard to make the most educated predictions I can. It’s a fine line between “all of our tech companies need to work extra hard to keep us secure” and “public infrastructure is actually going down.” It is very clear as of writing this that there are way more critical vulnerabilities which are being found in popular tools and fixes are being built. For example, Epoch AI recently published a nice post on their internal work using GLM-5.3 to try and find vulnerabilities and chain them into what could be an attack. The actual exploit they found in Firefox is a good example of why cyber risks need multiple things to align for harm to be done: We used GLM 5.3 to create a website that, simply when visited by a Firefox user and without further interaction, gave the attacker the ability to exfiltrate files from the user’s computer. Here, the exploit is in Firefox, and a would-be hacker needs to plant a website that is looking for this exploit. This is doable, and could have serious consequences, but just finding the exploit is only one step in a multi-stage process. In the previous post, I should’ve been more specific on what “fine” is for a future of cybersecurity, and in this case it means giving more credit to some of the AI safety community that discussed this reasonably as a new era in cyber instability. Reflecting on it,

items.title: Artificial Analysis v5 and the benchmarker's dilemma
items.content: Hill-climbing is easy, knowing what to hill-climb is hard. Making scores go up is expensive , but we have a much clearer playbook for it than we do for creating meaningful benchmarks at the true frontier of AI today. Independent evaluation of language models is under-appreciated in how hard of a task it is. These groups are not just taking current models and certifying their scores, which is a technically involved task. This is their job if AI progress is slow. When AI progress is as fast as it is, the technical details of the job are the routine work part of trying to put a single number on what makes for a good AI model today. The goal is to have a single number that is representative of current models, matching vibe checks, community sentiment, and scientific analysis, while being forward looking enough so that it’s not outdated in 3 months. Everyone building a benchmark faces a sort of paradox. You need your benchmark to reduce to one single number, so that it is easy to discuss, use in reports, and compare models, but every method of aggregating scores comes with meaningful trade-offs. The best scientists need to do this, everyone does. It’s a matter of creating aggregation metrics that you think are most fair, knowing there will always be imperfections. With the amount of money in the AI ecosystem today, the weight of independent evaluation is even higher – you dictate the winners and losers of a trillion dollar market. You also influence some of the models themselves, steering the shape of progress. This is a lot of pressure! My prompt for this article is Artificial Analysis’s recent update to their Intelligence Index, v5 . The AA index is the most prominent independent intelligence metric for the latest frontier models, followed in a distant second by Epoch AI’s Capabilities Index (ECI) . To date, all of these have been incredibly useful for the community and massively flawed! Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. Consider becoming a subscriber. Language models are capable of so much today, and this scope of capabilities is growing quickly. Our era of singular intelligence indices should be phased out soon, but it will take a long time. A summary of AAv5 is below, from their blog post, where they describe it as “reflecting real-world usage today:” Intelligence Index v5 weights: ➤ Knowledge Work (25%): AA-Briefcase (15%), AutomationBench-AA (5%), and GDP.pdf (5%) ➤ Coding (25%): FrontierCode 2.0 (15%) and Terminal-Bench 4.0 (10%) ➤ Science (25%): Terminal-Bench-Science (15%) and CritPt v2 hard subset (10%) ➤ General (25%): AA-Omniscience v1.1 15% (10% accuracy, 5% non-hallucination) and HLE-Diamond (10%) Here’s the new ranking of models: The problem with trying to benchmark real-world usage today is that it is extremely jagged, just like the models. The most proven use-case is coding, where open models are far more competitive and likely to keep up. In knowledge work, I’m less confident in open models. At first glance, in aggregate, their model ranking definitely looks reasonable. Still, it shows signs of strain and confusion, as any benchmark will, with GPT 6.1 Terra beating Claude Fable 5.1 on AAv5. Today, some benchmarks measure the absolute frontier of capabilities, playing nicely in open-ended tasks through your favorite harness, which often does take a large model. Some other benchmarks measure certain skills that will be needed of a model in repetitive agentic tasks. I get the feeling that AA is tuning their benchmark more towards the former, a general agentic collaborator, but all of these behaviors overlap. This takes us to the plot going around that prompted me to write this, where they showed the balance of open vs. closed models on the new benchmark. This plot shows 8 closed models beating the best to-be open-weight model, Kimi K3.1 Pro (which isn’t colored blue). This benchmark is taking the opinion of trying to measure where frontier models are moving into, which grows the gap to open models. This is an okay decision to take, but over time as existing workflows of open models become key factors of the economy, it could become a benchmark that misses where the core economic engine of the industry is. Open models’ demise from this seems greatly exaggerated, but I do think the previous index was flattering the open weight models too strongly. Consider this plot from the Kimi K3.1 Pro launch — yes, the open models are strong and useful in some cases, but the best OpenAI and Anthropic models have been a major step ahead in their flexibility and reliability. Some of the evaluations in AAv5 that open models are most behind on are “science” evals like terminal-bench-science and CritPT v2 . Open models are behind, but the value proposition was never to compete truly at the frontier. The open model economy will be about Reducing domains with high market demand for inference to a commodity price of hardware. Allowing ownership of intelligence, specializing it to internal data, and controlling internal agents across many companies in the economy. Both of these will take a very long time to materialize and are partially represented in benchmarks. The supply of compute is currently so low that open model providers also are raking in solid margins – when this shrinks, we will know the system is starting to work. The same goes for diffusion into enterprises, it’s not clear what the exact ceiling on it is because of the difficult ML expertise that is needed to build evaluations and do post-training today. Share At the next major model cycle, say in 2-3 months with GLM 6 or Kimi 3.5, I expect the leading open model labs to make substantial steps on this index, again surprising many observers. items.title: Podcast: Kimi K3.1 Pro, the new cyber reality, and Muse musings
items.content: We — Nathan and Florian — wanted to discuss all the messy trade-offs of a busy week in AI and ask all the pressing questions like: Why did Kimi K3.1 Pro have a mixed reaction with such incredible benchmarks? Will it be adopted? Were we wrong about the risks of open-weight models and cybersecurity? Why do cyber experts discuss recent events so differently than AI experts? What comes next in the few months? What will change our minds? We will write more about this subject, but wanted to bring you behind the curtain as we aspire to quickly learn more about the cybersecurity industry and trends across the last few years that have been leading us today. We conclude the podcast with some lighter topics, from Muse-maxing to excitement in still hiring junior technical talent. Please send us questions and topics, as we plan to record more of these podcasts going forward. Share Listen on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , and wherever you get your podcasts . For other Interconnects podcasts, go here . YouTube ↓ Chapters 00:00 Kimi K3.1 Reaction 08:15 Kimi’s open-weight cyber principles 11:23 You can hack everything era 15:54 PHP2Shell, LiteLLM, and the new internet 24:00 Abliterated APIs, safeguards, and trusted access 31:41 Anthropic not hiring juniors employees 36:16 Florian’s Muse addiction 45:30 Wrap-up Links we discuss My thread with Dean Ball about the “boy who cried wolf” story of the frontier labs Kimi K3.1 Pro announcement blog Kimi K3.1 Pro on Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index Kimi K3.1 on Artificial Analysis defensive cyber benchmarks Program Bench Open-weight Mythos would’ve been fine take PHP “hasn’t caused a disaster yet” update Abliteration.ai serving abliterated models API Morph serving abliterated DeepSeek via API Joshua Saxe’s Substack on AI and cybersecurity Azeem Azhar, “The internet’s Wuhan moment” Anthropic, “How employment is changing at Anthropic” LiteLLM security incident report Transcript 00:00:00 Nathan Lambert: We are back with another Interconnects podcast. We are with Florian, eval guy, recently moved to SF. Florian, is Kimi K3.1 Pro , name is a mouthful, going to live up to the benchmark scores, for example on Artificial Analysis , or where is it going to land? 00:00:17 Florian Brand: In the past, the Kimi models always lived up to the expectations, but this release is kind of weird compared to the others. I think it is also partially because they are becoming more professional, and the previous model drops were kind of out of nowhere. This time, which also got some criticism, they launched a bigger social media campaign, which allegedly also involved paying people to post about the model without disclosing. 00:00:56 Nathan Lambert: I think a lot of companies do this and tell you not to mention it, but it’s a mess. It’s bad form. No company should do it. Essentially, one person tweeted a screenshot of the press instructions for Kimi that said, “Don’t say this is a paid promotion.” And to my knowledge, no one has corroborated it after that. 00:01:15 Florian Brand: Yeah, and there are right now a few of these model launches, including by American companies, that are just very obviously astroturfed. We have seen launches where it’s thousands of retweets and a few hundred likes, because it works so well to get the attention. Some of them disclose that it is a paid ad while others don’t. But in general, we have seen the professionalization of model launches over time, and pretty quickly. A year ago, everyone just dropped the model, then patched vLLM afterwards, so no one was actually able to run any of the open models for a while. Now you get all the inference frameworks on day one, you get all the inference providers on day one. Or, which is also what we see more and more, the model creator has a few weeks of exclusive access before they release the weights. And that’s also what’s happening with K3.1 Pro. I think it’s two weeks of exclusive access before they release the model weights. 00:02:38 Nathan Lambert: They said the weights would come out by November 4th. And the headline things... I don’t know if I’m going to be able to share screen. I don’t have this set up on this computer. But the headline is this Artificial Analysis number where it’s ahead of GPT-6 Astra. And then if you look at the Kimi K3.1 blog, they have their headline numbers, which are really strong, and then they also have some numbers later on which seem a bit more jagged. I think it was Terminal-Bench Science , which is 20 points behind GPT-6 Astra. I think there were a few others, like ProgramBench . Do you know Terminal-Bench Science and ProgramBench? Are any of these things that people think are important benchmarks for frontier models? Or how do you explain the fact that on Artificial Analysis the model is top, what, three, four? It’s the two latest Claude 5.5 models, Muse Wonder Full, and then Kimi K3.1, which looks crazy. It just looks like totally crazy scores, and I think everybody is still surprised by it. But then there’s this long tail of details that you use to evaluate a model now. I had posted a thread on Twitter of, “What are people’s impressions?” And there’s a lot of people that are like, “This seems not great,” and then some people that are like, “Yeah, it’s fine.” I don’t know, there’s a mixed bag. Relative to K3, which I think was pretty unanimously, this feels like a big model and the post-training seemed a little bit undercooked for that. Maybe this is just a tiny bit RL fried. We’ll see where we land. 00:04:26 Florian Brand: For the benchmarks, one of the things is that the benchmarks that are right now used by Artificial Analysis, they will post their new version probably very soon after we release this podcast. 0

items.title: Latest open artifacts (#25): DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, American-made models, and new regulatory controls in the US & China
items.content: The geopolitics of open-weight AI are accelerating again this fall, as we would expect with the risks of all AI systems (open and closed) rising rapidly. We’ve seen many news items in the last week showing both the U.S. and Chinese governments positioning themselves for some controls on open models. MOFCOM, the Ministry of Commerce of the People’s Republic of China, released a policy proposal (it’s not yet a law) that would require frontier AI models and some other technologies to get pre-approval from the government before they can be shared internationally. We found the reaction to this to be overblown – as the document states that open-source technologies will be set up for automatic approvals – but many in geopolitical circles say this is a big deal because it proposes a regulatory framework that could be used in the future to regulate China’s AI industry. Others we trust on this issue say this proposal could be more about preventing issues like the sale of Chinese startup Manus to Western companies, rather than being about frontier AI models. Either way, the wheels of control are moving around AI, and open-weight models are not free from any influence. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released an order on DeepSeek , which restricts DeepSeek itself, as a company, and DeepSeek’s models, as a technology platform, from being a vendor in federal civilian procurement. It is not clear how this will relate to finetuned models or models trained on the outputs of DeepSeek (e.g., Nvidia’s Nemotron models have long relied heavily on DeepSeek models in their training recipes – will they be banned?), but this is an expected action and reinforces the need for a domestic open model ecosystem. Other model makers in China, such as Zhipu AI, makers of GLM, are already on the Entity List under Commerce/BIS, which restricts their access to American technology. DeepSeek followed the above news up by releasing their internal inference stack publicly, DeepInfer , which is likely far more efficient than existing open-source tools like vLLM/SGLang for their models. Estimates point to DeepSeek making up to 90% gross margin when selling tokens on this inference stack. It is well-known that the top AI labs have much more inference-efficient tools internally, and this is the first time we’ve seen a leading lab share them. Inference companies will be quick to adopt these tools, which will drive prices for DeepSeek’s models down across the ecosystem (or margins up). While not an open model or dataset, we consider this release to be one of the bigger open-source AI artifacts in the last few months. Share As of writing this, Kimi K3.1 is rumored to be released very soon, with metadata associated with it starting to appear in public libraries . Exciting times! You can view the models in this email, and all previous issues, on our Artifacts Hub. It includes commentary and other ecosystem metadata. Browse the Artifacts Hub Our Picks MiMo-V2.6-Pro-RL by XiaomiMiMo : an update for Mimo, which reuses the same bases as MiMo V2.5, but used a lot more resources on RL training. They also release an in-depth tech report , as well as some of the used environments, which is rare at this scale. The final model from this recipe, V2.6-Pro, is the top open model on Artificial Analysis’s ranking today, and the scaled RL runs came with a fun live dashboard of training. We’ve been fans of Xiaomi for months now, and their efforts are bearing fruit. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 by deepseek-ai : Since the latest Artifacts, the whale has not released one, but two new model iterations with a new size (552B-A16B) which also support image inputs. The model has gained a lot of (well-deserved) attention for its performance at a small price. It also carries the MIT license, continuing the trend established by DeepSeek themselves. This is notable in times where licenses seem to become more bespoke and exclusionary. Below is the Pareto of performance vs price on DeepSWE, a favorite agentic software engineering benchmark today, which DeepSeek dominates. clef by Cloudflare : Decision models are all the rage after being introduced by the startup Typesafe . In short, they are general classification models that output few tokens with their probabilities. Its usefulness has led to quick adoption and also a lot of open model finetunes such as Clef. NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4 by nvidia : The mid-sized model of the Nemotron family got its long awaited update. It is strong for its size and can be run at home (given you own a beefy laptop or RTX Spark). As usual, NVIDIA releases the vast majority of the data and an in-depth tech report . Beam-1.0-501B-A23B by reflection : The long awaited open model by Reflection, making it the strongest open American model released under a permissive license (Apache 2.0). While not the smartest open model available, Beam is very impressively token efficient (second to only GPT-6-Astra below). This is a sign of a well-developed post-training stack. Models General Purpose Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf by prism-ml : A ternary version of Qwen3.8-27B for on-device deployments. Ornith-1.5-397B by ornith-ai : A series of Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4 finetunes that gained attention in the local AI community for its strong performance over the respective (strong) baselines. Ling-3.0-flash-VL-fp4 by inclusionAI : A 124B-A5.5B model by Ant Ling (within Ant Group), which continues to churn out models consistently. Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B by meta-models : META has released their open version of Muse, which we have written about in more detail ! Read more

items.title: Meta shakes up the frontiers, open and closed
items.content: This has been a week where the balance of American open-weight models took a step change back toward the frontier. Meta took the lead of this charge with Muse Spark Open , which is now the strongest American-made open model by quite some margin, but the addition of Reflection’s first model Beam is also relevant. Without these two models, there would be 20+ open-weight models built and released by Chinese companies better than the best Western models. At the time of writing this, Mistral has also announced a strong model, Mistral Large 4 , with an index score of 38 (see below), but its weights are not yet released. There are rumors of a few more strong American open-weight models coming from other organizations too! In many ways, the gap between the best American and Chinese models has been reduced roughly by half. We’ve gone from the best American open models being largely irrelevant to consumers who require the cutting edge of performance, to them being behind but relevant. This paints the picture of the cut-throat, competitive nature of the frontier model business. Reflection and Mistral announced their model scores and Meta dropped the weights of a smarter model before these other two labs could get their own weights out. All of these models are competing with Chinese models released months ago, where the industry is collectively asking — where have Kimi and Zhipu AI been since the releases of GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3 on Aug. 18th and Jul. 16th, respectively? That is a very nuanced question, which I’ll dig into another time. Today’s piece is focused on Meta’s turnaround, what Muse Spark Open means for the ecosystem, and the balance of power across Western frontier labs. Share Why Muse Spark Open should take off — and why it may not One thing we see again and again at Interconnects through our open model analysis is that Western open-weight models get astonishingly more adoption than Chinese models with the same performance-to-size footprint (even though the Chinese models usually come out first)! Muse Spark Open is landing into this environment, at the same time as when open-ended LLM agents are finally real (~ GLM 5.2 capabilities and on ). Riding off a rapid increase in performance of Chinese models, the open ecosystem has been living through an acceleration in demand. The inference providers are rapidly scaling, the open post-training economy is forming, and countless enterprises are looking to own their intelligence. Muse Spark Open’s performance falls somewhere above GLM 5.2, near DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and behind GLM 5.3 or Kimi K3. It should be squarely “good enough” to slot right into this. For some background, from the Muse Spark Open model card on Hugging Face: Muse Spark Open is an 816B total/42B active parameter open weights model with a context window of 1M tokens. Built for coding and agentic work, Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal. This open weights version has additional safety post-training to make it more robust against misuse as a standalone model without system guardrails. We recommend deploying Muse Spark Open as part of a broader AI system, with additional guardrails suited to the specific use case. Here’s the distribution of the various Muse models on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. This is included to loop back to the original model card snippet. It was shared that this open-weight model underwent additional safety training to prepare for this open release. Many observers saw this release as potentially a model that was “broken” during the safety training, as it came out after Muse Spark 1.3. In reality, this was much more likely a safety tune of Muse Spark 1.2, which would only be a 1 point drop on Artificial Analysis to shore up safety behaviors. When Meta released Muse Glimmer , the 30B agentic model, Alex Wang said that they were preparing to release the Muse Spark 1.2 model as open weights, which fits with the above. If anything will hold Muse Spark Open back, it’ll be the specific license they designed for it. In summary, this custom license has pretty much all of the restrictive license behaviors we’ve seen (and criticized here) in the last few years of building with open models. They are as follows: Users of the models in products must display “Built with Muse” on their products. Meta did this with Llama, and Kimi has tried it, but almost no one complies. There is a revenue-gating factor, where companies that make more than $20M per month across their entire business deploying the model need a separate license with Meta. Other prominent open model providers are doing this too, in order to set up revenue share agreements for re-selling inference. Muse Spark Open makes you agree to an acceptable use policy, which in the true “open source software” corner of the world makes this model extremely not open-source. All of the above applies to outputs from the model as well, and derivatives, so there is legal ambiguity if you can safely use the model for synthetic data. The license does permit using Muse Spark Open for internal research and applications. We’re at a weird equilibrium where this license is complex and unproven in court, but many players will likely ignore it. Many, many people will build on this model from various inference providers, and Meta will only likely go after egregious violations. For now, licenses haven’t been the determining factor of AI adoption, but this could change in the future. This is why we think it’s an unnecessary strategic risk for labs trying to compete and regain adoption to have complex, non-standard open licenses for their models. items.title: I expect rapid progress but not towards general superintelligence
items.content: I’ve often been surprised when I hear from top researchers in industry that they think AI will be better than them at their job in a few years, and I didn’t really know why I doubted it. The explanation I arrived at is that researchers are seeing this massive acceleration in the infra and engineering capabilities of the models. I fully agree that the models will be superhuman distributed GPU engineers in a few years. This will make experimentation and tinkering with the formulation of the models far easier, but it will not make our models dramatically different in nature. In some ways, Ilya was early in his declaration of AI being in the era of research . Research is much easier today now that we have coding agents. This ease is through a different form of work that is flexible and engaging, which signals the start of an era where good ideas can be much more valuable than good execution in software. Subscribe now We’re very early on this path. It’s also not the first transition the field has seen across the balance in if AI is more “research” or “engineering.” Before deep learning took off, AI was also far more of a research endeavor. Today, the best researchers are well-known to be judged by their ability to implement and scale their ideas in complex infrastructure. We’re about to go through a massive acceleration over a few years where the bottleneck is less and less engineering again. Some call this RSI, but a more grounded form is simply “parallelized, AI-assisted language modeling.” You don’t need to buy into takeoff scenarios to see just how much infrastructure improvements are coming, and how this’ll change the nature of working in AI. The goal of this piece is to give an overview on why this engineering acceleration will happen, and touch on what it won’t quite fix. This’ll be a massive boon for diffusion of the technology into the economy, even if we don’t get economically valuable superhuman traits outside of math and coding. A lot of this near-term progress comes from scaling the inference-time compute we have with current tools, rather than dramatic step-changes in how good the models are at research. Share Many pieces of the AI training and inference stack are very verifiable. Training metrics like tokens per second per GPU, which is just training speed. Inference metrics look like tokens per prompt, FLOPs per token, or really just cost per answer. Both of these are very optimizable, especially as there are established sub-problems and architecture trade-offs which can improve them. I expect AI agents to help optimize this process end-to-end in a few years, where our inference capabilities get very close to the underlying maximum compute possible on our accelerators like GPUs. Over the previous few years, the gains companies can make on inference efficiency were already giant, e.g. saving like 10-30% on cost to serve a model after announcing it at a certain price point. This entire stack will compound, and I expect the effective cost of model intelligence to decline near-exponentially over the coming years (potentially faster than recent trends). This low-hanging fruit of efficiency should take only a few years to capture. The longer term will be co-design of accelerators and models on longer timelines, which give extra orders of magnitude in efficiency on top of the flexible GPU platform. During this time of rapid efficiency gains, the flexibility of the GPU should be king, as the exploration space in architecture feels important and like a major lever of automated research. A prediction of pretraining research, at least in architecture and data selection to serve our current class of models, being automated in 2-3 years feels reasonable to me. All of this will be a massive trigger of Jevons paradox for agentic models. I expect demand to only increase, as the industry is largely bottlenecked on figuring out better ways to orient and deliver the agents. Meta’s Muse agent is an early indicator of this and we should expect more Muse-like experiences for different audiences and target use-cases. It’s value created by understanding how agents work, rather than pushing the frontier of performance. The equivalent phase in the broader scientific literature like biology and chemistry will be an era defined by models finding numerous cross-sub-field findings. The AI models are superhuman at crawling literature and making connections across sparse networks which are currently stewarded by small communities of scientists who rarely interacted. There will be a fine line between this heralding a new era of scientific discovery, e.g. with cures of most cancers, or an acceleration of the arc science was already on. Another industrial-scale piece of low-hanging fruit is improving the general quality of RL environments. You don’t have to look far to see another new RL data company that’s crossed $100M or $1B in revenue. There are way more than I expected. The average outputs from this sector are remarkably low-quality. Countless researchers agree that lots of what they buy is frankly crap. At the same time, the leading labs see clear return on investment from buying the data. The way that many RL environments are cruddy is clearly fixable. Read more

items.title: The Cyber Risk Discourse is Broken
items.content: I’ve had one too many discussions on the cyber risks of open models — where someone assumes that either banning open models happens in a silo (and bad actors will somehow actually be stopped) or that China is a threat and doesn’t care about AI safety — that I feel we’re going to end up making policy decisions that both limit American AI competitiveness and increases long-term cyber risk. I feel like we’re locked in on a path of lose-lose situation, unless people embrace nuance, trade-offs, and scary realities. Much has been written about the views of various players in this debate, which I summarize as follows: Open weight models pose an untenable risk to society’s functionality , occupied by frontier lab leadership and the national security community in the U.S. Western voices saying open weight models are necessary for defense and banning them will make the world less safe , occupied by AI risk moderates to different extremes. I include myself in this bucket, along with Hugging Face’s perspective after the OpenAI incident, and others like Joshua Saxe . Chinese companies continuing to release open-weight models with strong cyber capabilities , who are making decisions based on the risk assessments of their society and government. This list is also organized by volume or clarity of message in the Western AI ecosystem. The risk-focused discussions have been disproportionately visible, including pieces of work which I view as very detrimental to potential of engaging across assumed party lines on this issue. There’s also very little substantive engagement trying to understand how Chinese companies assess risk — rather, mostly arguments that border on ad hominem attacks like “Chinese labs don’t care about safety.” Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. Consider becoming a subscriber. The delusions of the anti open-weight alliance The most recent publication from the “open-weights are dangerous” crowd was the report by Anthropic on the risks of GLM-5.3 as an offensive cyber tool. The problem with this is not the technical research they did, which is largely reasonable, but the failure to engage on more cross cutting questions like: What happens if we ban open models due to cyber risks or why do Chinese companies deem these models safe to release? These questions, which I’ll come back to, are the ones we need to answer to understand the ecosystem perspective on current AI risks. All policy actions happen in a multi-piece puzzle, where the shape of risk can be changed, but it is rare that you get a universally better outcome. They are all trade-offs. This sort of solipsistic writing by Anthropic fits very closely to another type of discourse I’m hearing about regularly that is determining the fate of open models and AI broadly — classified briefings. I’ve had many discussions with people who say something like “Look, I’m pro open models, but if you’re seeing what I’m seeing, it’s an onslaught out there due to [XYZ Chinese open-weight model] and we need to act.” This perspective flies in the face of public information, where to date closed models have been documented as the cause of most existing cyber attacks. As someone who tries to make grounded predictions, the evidence of numerous attacks from OpenAI models is the only data I have on the shape of cyber risks (or, you can broaden the scope to include all of FelonyBench ). There are a few possible explanations, and it’ll take years to get to the true answer: Maybe open model weights and closed model APIs (with some safe guards) are both far closer to being easy to mis-use, rather than API models being closer to safe. The trope "Open Dangerous, Closed Safe" may be closer to "Open Unsafe, Closed Unsafe." Maybe there are far fewer bad actors who are willing to use AI models for “loud” cyber attacks that target crucial infrastructure in the US or powerful and underprepared institutions. Closed models have stronger capabilities and stronger safeguards (in theory), but the stronger capabilities part could matter more in net harm if the safeguards on both are porous. I have a lot more to learn about how the cybersecurity ecosystem works, so I won’t support this full-heartedly as one of my current recommendations, but I think it’s at least a reasonable argument that open weight models as a diffusion tool for cyber defense could be the best tool we have to prevent harm over the next few years. There are many domains, e.g. sensitive government agencies, where open-weight models are the only tools that can be deployed in the near-term on air-gapped networks. Lots of this situation seems like the messy reality being hard to pin down, where the logical limits are clearer. I may agree with the simple reality that closed models are far safer in the limit, as a technical tool with more layers of protection, but they may actually be causing more harm in the near term because of how accessible model APIs are. Still, much of the impact of the tools comes down to how they’re used and controlled. A duopoly on such a crucial tool may be the defining, risky part. This is the debate we’re having, and over time, as intelligence diffuses, many things may change. These together make me come to the conclusion that if you think the latest open-weight models need to be banned to slow the diffusion of cyber risks, you probably also need to make public-facing APIs for the frontier closed-models illegal. The current stack of safeguards on closed models is stronger than open-weight models, but far from perfect. It is very likely that cyber capabilities of closed models increase much faster than guardrail performance, and a world where open models are banned while closed models continue to progress would be increasing the offense-defense cyber gap.
